items.text: One mortgage passes through a lot of hands, and each one has a narrow job. The roles sound alike — broker, lender, servicer — and that's where nearly all the early confusion comes from. Exam writers know it too. Expect to be asked which one did what.

The borrower takes the loan and pledges the home. The mortgage loan originator — the M-L-O, the job you're studying for — is the licensed professional who takes the application and offers or negotiates the loan's terms. Hold onto that phrase exactly as it stands: takes an application, and offers or negotiates terms. It's the statutory test for who needs a license at all, and it comes back in Module Four. The M-L-O is also the borrower's main point of contact the whole way through. The M-L-O works for a broker or a lender, and that employer is where the next distinction begins.

A mortgage broker arranges the loan — shopping the application among several lenders to find a fit — but never puts up the money. The lender, sometimes called the creditor, is the party that actually funds it. The money going to the closing table is the lender's. The servicer manages the loan after closing: collecting the monthly payment, running escrow, sending statements. And the servicer is often a completely different company than the lender. Servicing rights can be bought and sold like any other asset, which is why a borrower's payment address can change even though nothing about their loan did.

The rest of the work falls to a handful of specialists, each with a single job. The loan processor assembles and organizes the file — documents, verifications — but decides nothing. Hold that line, because the processor-versus-underwriter swap is one of the most reliable wrong answers on the exam. The underwriter measures that file against the program's guidelines and makes the approve-or-deny call. The appraiser gives an independent opinion of the home's value, and that independence is legally protected — nobody on the deal may lean on it. The title company searches the title and issues title insurance. At the table, the settlement agent — often the title company or an attorney — runs the closing and disburses the funds. Separately, the real estate agent represents the buyer or the seller in the purchase itself. And notice the money runs sideways to the borrower's payment: the appraiser is paid for the appraisal but stays independent of the result, the agents earn commission out of the sale, and the servicer collects a fee for managing the loan.
